title: Astronomers Discover Cotton-Candy Planets That Defy Explanation
summary:
Imagine a planet so light it could float in a giant bathtub. Astronomers have discovered two Jupiter-sized exoplanets that are less dense than cotton candy. Named TOI-791 b and TOI-791 c, they orbit a Sun-like star about 1,113 light-years from Earth. These rare worlds belong to a class called "super-puffs."

"Only a handful of these super-puffy planets are known, and it is even rarer to find two in the same system," said Dr. George Dransfield, who led the study. "Their extremely low densities make them fascinating targets for understanding how planetary systems form and evolve."

The discovery began with volunteers analyzing data from NASA's TESS space telescope. They spotted tiny dips in a star's brightness, hinting that planets were passing in front of it. To confirm, Dr. Dransfield's team used telescopes worldwide. The ASTEP observatory in Antarctica proved crucial because the continuous darkness of the Antarctic winter allowed them to record several complete transits. Each transit—when a planet crosses its star and blocks light—lasted over 11 hours, the longest ever observed from the ground.

By measuring changes in starlight during transits, the team determined the planets' sizes. They calculated masses by observing how the planets' gravity affected each other's orbits. Together, these measurements revealed extremely low densities.

The two planets orbit in a resonant pattern: for every five orbits of the inner planet, the outer completes three. This suggests they formed together from the same disk of gas and dust. The findings were published in the Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society on June 25, 2026.

Scientists still don't know how super-puffs form. One leading theory: they have large hydrogen and helium atmospheres around small solid cores, making them appear huge but keeping density low. Dr. Dransfield's team hopes to study their atmospheres with the James Webb Space Telescope to solve the mystery.
why_it_matters: Super-puffs show that planet formation can produce worlds our models barely predict, and understanding how those atmospheres and orbits behave helps scientists judge which distant planets could ever support life — and how unusual our own solar system really is.

background_read: Super-puffs are among the rarest planets astronomers know. The most famous examples were found in the Kepler-51 system in the early 2010s by NASA's Kepler space telescope, and only a handful have been confirmed since — which is why finding two in one system is so unusual.

The data came from NASA's TESS (the Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite, launched in 2018 to watch bright nearby stars for planets passing in front of them). The Antarctic telescope ASTEP (Antarctic Search for Transiting ExoPlanets) is operated from Concordia Station at Dome C, where months of unbroken night make long, continuous observations possible.

Planets that are light for their size are usually explained by thick hydrogen and helium envelopes wrapped around small solid cores. Astronomers also use resonance as a clue to a planet system's history: in our own solar system, Neptune and Pluto share a 3-to-2 rhythm, and three of Jupiter's moons move in a locked 4-to-2-to-1 pattern.

The James Webb Space Telescope, which began observing in 2022, can analyse the chemistry of a planet's atmosphere as the planet passes in front of its star — the tool the team now wants to use to solve the super-puff mystery.

perspectives.description: Planetary scientists see this as a lucky find: a rare class of planet, two of them in one system, plus volunteers and a polar telescope working together. The 5-to-3 resonance gives a strong clue that the pair were born together, and the James Webb Space Telescope can now try to read their atmospheres.

Some researchers would note that only a handful of super-puffs are known, so any conclusions rest on a very small sample. The masses come indirectly, from how the planets nudge each other, and the light, puffy structure is exactly the kind of thing that is hard to confirm. Interesting, but not yet a settled explanation.

Astronomers have been surprised before: the first 'hot Jupiter' found in the 1990s broke the textbook rules about where giant planets can orbit, and it forced the whole field to rewrite its formation models. Super-puffs are the newest puzzle of the same kind — a reminder that our theories are built from a small number of examples.

The next test is spectroscopy: measuring which wavelengths of starlight the planets' atmospheres absorb as they pass in front of their star. If the team finds the expected hydrogen and helium, the thick-envelope theory gains support; if not, scientists may need an entirely new way to explain how a planet can be as light as cotton candy.
